extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of poetics and tragic playwriting (classics, dramaturgy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama (plot, character, recognition, diction, metre). Focuses on how to structure action, produce recognition/reversal, shape characters, and use language and metrical elements for tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of plot (beginning–middle–end;δέσις and λύσις)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy must have a unified structure with a binding portion (from the start until the turning point) and a solution (from the turning-point to the end). The plot should form a single integrated whole rather than a disconnected sequence of episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the plot moves from a clear beginning through a causal middle to a satisfying end; avoid assembling an epic-length collection of episodes. Compose both the knot (δέσις) and the untying (λύσις) so that they correspond and resolve together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events should be probable or necessary (avoid the irrational within the action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions and outcomes in the drama must follow from necessity or probability; irrational or incredible elements should not be included within the play itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If something irrational must appear, place it outside the action (e.g., as report, deus-ex-machina explanation, or divine vision). Keep causal chains believable and rooted in the situation and characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis) ideally from the action itself
rubrics_metrics.description: The best kind of recognition is that which is caused by events and deeds of the plot itself (recognition arising from action), producing surprise and emotional power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer recognitions that emerge naturally from what characters do rather than contrived tokens or external explanations. Examples: Sophocles' Oedipus and Iphigenia where recognition follows action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of recognition (ranked and described)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions occur by various means: by signs/tokens, by artificial contrivances, by recollection (memory), and by inference/argumentation; some are more artful or effective than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer: (1) recognition from deeds (best), (2) recognition by signs/tokens (strong when authentic, e.g., scar), (3) recollection or memory, (4) recognition by plausible inference or sophistic argument (weaker). Avoid recognitions produced solely by theatrical trickery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal (peripeteia) combined with recognition produces strongest effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A reversal in fortune that coincides with or is followed by recognition produces the most powerful tragic experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the plot so that a peripeteia (sudden change of circumstances) leads into, or is linked with, anagnorisis to maximize surprise and emotional impact. The best ending is one where the agent acts ignorantly, then recognizes after the deed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/status of agent: avoid the worst pattern (knowing and not acting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Among possible moral/volitional configurations, the worst (most ugly and non-tragic) is an agent who knows the course of action and fails to act; better are actions done in ignorance with later recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For tragic dignity and moral sympathy, prefer characters who act in ignorance and then recognize (this produces pity/fear) rather than characters who knowingly refrain or commit ugly acts without awareness of their significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (ἦθος) — four evaluative aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: When shaping characters consider: (1) goodness (chrestos) — characters should be fundamentally good; (2) fitness/appropriateness — traits must fit the character's social/gender/role; (3) similarity/consistency — character traits should be coherent and not arbitrary; (4) normality/homogeneity (ὁμαλόν) — even abnormal characters should be represented consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters appropriate to their role (e.g., avoid making a woman display ‘manly’ courage that is unfitting), keep internal consistency, and if portraying wickedness, distinguish between necessary evil and gratuitous depravity. Use examples (e.g., Homer's Achilles, Euripides' depictions) to guide tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of customary behaviour (consuetudo) to ground plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Character actions and plots should arise from customary behaviours that are (1) good, (2) fitting, (3) similar to the kind of person portrayed, and (4) equitable or proportionate — these customs help make the story credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure actions reflect believable social norms and conventional behaviors for the person’s class/gender/status; customs are a tool for making motives and consequences intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contrived theatrical devices for recognition (prefer natural tokens)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions or plot-resolving devices that result from theatrical contrivance (manufactured signs, improbable mechanisms) are inferior to recognitions that arise authentically from action or plausible tokens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using a token (e.g., necklace, scar), prefer those that would credibly exist and be noticed; avoid purely invented stage tricks that break probability or audience belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of noble/typical characters (mimesis of appropriate exemplars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poet should imitate admirable or representative characters (like skilled painters imitate fine models), producing credible depictions of traits (e.g., Achilles’ hardness) suited to the poet's aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose exemplars whose traits the audience can recognize and whose imitation will generate the intended emotional and moral responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show rather than tell; make the action visible and vivid
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots and diction should be worked so that what is most central is put before the eyes — the poet should set things before sight to make them most clear and avoid hiding opposites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose scenes and speeches so that the audience ‘sees’ the events and feelings, thereby making the appropriate responses (pity, fear) more immediate and less dependent on explanatory narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode length appropriate to dramatic form (brevity in drama)
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes in drama should be short and compact; epic can sustain long narratives and many episodes, but drama needs concise episodes that serve the unified plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the epicizing tendency (epopoeic style) in tragedy; keep episodes tight and focused on the central action to maintain dramatic intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid composing tragedy like an epic (do not be epopoeic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy should not be a long-story epic relocated to the stage; excessive narrative multiplicity or length undermines tragic focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist creating a play that attempts to cover an entire epic tale; instead concentrate on a coherent portion of events that will function dramatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration and role of the chorus
rubrics_metrics.description: The chorus should be treated as a component part of the dramatic whole — effectively one of the actors and a participant in the contest of the play (properly integrated, as in Sophocles rather than the manner of Euripides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the chorus to contribute to the unity of the piece (emotionally, thematically, and metrically) rather than as an unrelated interlude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to produce pity and fear by properly preparing passions
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must prepare and present passions (pity, fear, anger, etc.) through both action (the plot) and diction (speeches) so that the audience experiences these responses legitimately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plot events, character choices, and well-crafted speech to arouse emotions; some effects should appear without explicit teaching, others must be prepared through language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and figures of speech are essential (knowledge of rhetorical forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet must know the figures and forms of speech (imperative, prayer, narration, threat, question, answer, etc.) and the architectonics of acting-speech (ὑποκριτική) to avoid error and to craft effective lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mastery of rhetorical forms is a necessary part of poetic craft; ignorance of these devices is rightfully criticized when a poet fails in creating proper verbal effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of phonetic and metrical elements appropriate to effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Sound-elements (vowels, semi-vowels, non-vowels), syllable composition, conjunctions, articles, names, verbs, cases, and sentence structure must be considered relative to metrical needs and intended tonal/metrical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to how sounds combine (vowel+consonant for syllables; semi-vowels; consonantal units), to accent/length, to sharpness and heaviness in voice — all of which affect meter and dramatic delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical composition of syllables and metres
rubrics_metrics.description: A syllable is a composed meaningful sound (vowel + consonant); metrical differences depend on mouth shape, place, roughness, smoothness, length, shortness, and pitch; proper composition is required for metrical accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets must understand which consonant-vowel combinations form syllables in their metrics (e.g., G+R without A is not a syllable), and how to deploy them to meet metrical patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot species and preference for the complex plot
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four species of tragedy: complex (with reversal and recognition), the pathetical (events), the ethical (based on character), and the ‘proper’/mythic (e.g., Prometheus). The complex plot, with peripeteia and anagnorisis, is generally the most effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for complex plots where possible; where not feasible, attempt to secure the greatest possible portion of the crucial elements (reversal/recognition) to achieve tragic impact.
